patent: Filed 1989-07-17 and issued 1990-08-14 to Jack L. Jewell and Axel Scherer of Bell Communications Research (Bellcore). It describes an electrically pumped vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser (VCSEL) a few micrometres across: an InGaAs quantum-well active region between two epitaxial AlAs/GaAs Bragg mirrors, all grown in one molecular beam epitaxy run (504 layers, about 5.3 um), capped with gold, then etched into free-standing pillars by chemically assisted xenon ion beam etching. Two practical points carry the design: short-period superlattices graded between the mirror layers to lower the series resistance of the p and n mirrors, and a low-damage etch so that sidewall defects do not dominate pillars only 2 to 5 um wide. Because In_{0.2}Ga_{0.8}As emits at a longer wavelength than GaAs absorbs, the light leaves through the GaAs substrate. The tested 3 um device lased at 958 nm with a 1.3 mA threshold (FIG. 10). The same work was published as J. L. Jewell et al., "Low-threshold electrically pumped vertical-cavity surface-emitting microlasers", Electronics Letters, 1989. The VCSEL itself goes back to K. Iga's group (H. Soda et al., Japanese Journal of Applied Physics, 1979); this patent's contribution is the micrometre-scale, strongly index-guided, electrically pumped pillar.

figs.1: The whole device in one section, not to scale. The pillar 12 (arrow at top) is the stack 14 to 24 standing on the n+ substrate 10; its rounded feet meet the substrate surface. The contact 26 touches the gold on top and the contact 28 touches the substrate. The wavy arrow under the substrate is the laser output, which leaves downward through the lower mirror and the substrate.
figs.2: The bottom part of the stack: the substrate 10 at the bottom, the lower mirror 14 above it, the lower spacer 16, and the start of the graded layer 64 at the top. Only the first and last of the twenty mirror periods 28 are drawn; the dots stand for the rest. The bottom period is labelled in full: AlAs 30, a 6.8 nm superlattice 34 and GaAs 32. Here the numeral 28 means a mirror period, not the substrate contact of FIG. 1. The jagged sides mean the layers continue sideways. The printed 24.33 nm for the superlattice 44 does not match FIG. 4, whose layer thicknesses add up to 21.51 nm.
figs.3: A close-up of the superlattice 34 that sits between the AlAs layer 30 (below) and the GaAs layer 32 (above) in every lower mirror period: two 1.7 nm GaAs layers 36 and two 1.7 nm AlAs layers 38. The text does not explain the curved arrow labelled 18 at the lower left. In the text, 18 is the quantum well region, which is not in this figure.
figs.4: A close-up of the lower spacer superlattice 44 between the AlAs layer 40 (below) and the Al_{0.5}Ga_{0.5}As layer 42 (above). The AlGaAs layers 56 all stay at 1.7 nm while the GaAs layers get thinner upward (50: 1.7 nm, 52: 1.13 nm, 54: 0.56 nm), so the average composition moves from GaAs-like at the bottom toward AlGaAs at the top. Read the stack from the bottom: the growth goes upward.
figs.5: The active region 18, read from the bottom: the graded layer 64 (Al_{0.5}Ga_{0.5}As grading to GaAs), then three 8 nm InGaAs wells 60 between four 10 nm GaAs barriers 62, then the graded layer 66 (GaAs back to AlGaAs). The arrows in the right-hand labels show the direction of grading. The lower spacer layer 42 is below and the upper spacer 20 is above.
figs.6: The top part of the stack, from the upper spacer 20 (above the graded layer 66) to the gold 24. Each mirror period 70 is, from the bottom: superlattice 76 (4.52 nm), AlAs 72 (68 nm), superlattice 78 (22.6 nm) and GaAs 74 (57 nm). Only the first and last of the twelve periods are drawn; the dots stand for the rest. Above the last full period, the mirror ends with superlattice 76, a thinner 27 nm AlAs layer 104, superlattice 78 and a 3 nm GaAs contact layer 106 under the gold.
figs.7: A close-up of the 4.52 nm superlattice 76, which sits between a GaAs layer 74 (below) and an AlAs layer 72 (above) in each upper mirror period: alternating 1.13 nm AlAs layers 80 and GaAs layers 82.
figs.8: A close-up of the 22.6 nm superlattice 78 between the AlAs layer 72 (below) and the GaAs layer 74 (above). The brackets on the right pair the labels into five two-period sections. In the drawing the composition is aluminium-rich at the bottom (AlAs 86 with 0.56 nm Al_{0.5}Ga_{0.5}As 84) and gallium-rich at the top (1.7 nm GaAs 100 with AlGaAs 102), so each end matches the layer it touches. The text describes the grading the other way round ("GaAs-rich ... at the bottom to an AlAs-rich one at the top"), but the drawing and the listed layers agree with each other.
figs.9: A schematic of the etching chamber 110. The sample 116 sits on the heated holder 120 and faces the ion source 128 on the right. The Cl_{2} gas from the tube 122 comes out through the two hook-shaped nozzles 124 aimed at the sample face. The load-lock 118 at the top has a long transfer rod (not numbered) running down to the holder. The mass spectrometer 126 samples the chamber, and the pumping stack 114 with its valve symbol is at the bottom. The text does not describe the drawing inside the source 128.
figs.10: Light output against drive current for the 3 um pillar at 958 nm, measured with 50 ns pulses. The output is close to zero below about 1.3 mA and then rises roughly linearly to about 0.46 mW at 3.5 mA. The lowest mark on the output axis is printed "0.5"; since the marks go up in steps of 0.1 mW, it should read 0.

parts.28: The patent uses this numeral for two things: the substrate contact in FIG. 1 ("electrical contact", later "lower lead" and "lower contact") and one mirror period of the lower mirror in FIG. 2.
parts.104: The text first calls this the 27 nm AlAs layer and then says "The GaAs layer 104 was delta-doped". The delta-doped top contact layer is evidently the 3 nm GaAs layer 106.
parts.34: The short-period superlattices (34, 44, 76, 78) smooth the abrupt band offset at each AlAs/GaAs interface. This lowers the voltage drop across the many heterointerfaces in the doped mirrors.
parts.18: In FIGS. 1 and 5, 18 is the active region with three quantum wells. FIG. 3 also has a numeral 18 with an arrow, which the text does not explain.
parts.26: In the tested samples this contact was a movable probe with a tip radius of about 5 um that touched the gold on top of the pillar.
parts.128: A gridded broad-beam ion source, here producing a 1000 eV Xe^{+} beam.

glossary.def: Vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser: the laser cavity runs perpendicular to the wafer and is closed by two epitaxial mirrors, so the light leaves through the top or bottom surface instead of a cleaved edge.

A stack of alternating high- and low-index layers, each a quarter of the wavelength thick in its material. The reflections add in phase and give reflectivity near 100% over a band of wavelengths. Also called a distributed Bragg reflector (DBR).
A semiconductor layer only a few nanometres thick, between layers with a wider bandgap. It traps electrons and holes, and its emission wavelength depends on both its composition and its thickness.
A layer between the active region and a mirror. Its thickness sets the cavity length (here one wavelength) and places the wells at the peak of the standing-wave field.

A periodic stack of very thin layers (about 1 nm here). In this patent, short-period AlAs/GaAs/AlGaAs superlattices are used to grade the composition between mirror layers. The drawings label them SL.
A layer whose AlGaAs composition changes gradually through its thickness. Here it confines carriers near the wells and gives a smoother potential than an abrupt step.
Heavily doped p-type or n-type semiconductor. Here n+ uses silicon (Si) as the donor and p+ uses beryllium (Be) as the acceptor, at a few 10^{18} cm^{-3}.
Putting dopant into a single atomic plane, by stopping growth while only the dopant source is open. It gives a very high local doping density, which here produces a low-resistance contact.
Molecular beam epitaxy: crystal growth in ultra-high vacuum from beams of evaporated elements, with monolayer control of layer thickness.

Dry etching in which an inert-gas ion beam (here xenon) hits the sample while a reactive gas (here chlorine) flows over it. The chemistry helps remove material, so less ion energy is needed and the etch causes less damage than physical milling alone.

A gridded broad-beam ion source of the type developed by Harold Kaufman. A hot-filament discharge in a magnetic field ionizes the gas, and grids extract and accelerate the ions. The usual spelling is "Kaufman".
A small chamber that is pumped down on its own, so samples can be moved into a vacuum chamber without venting it.
Standard cubic centimetres per minute, a unit of gas flow.
The drive current above which stimulated emission takes over and the output power starts rising steeply with current (the knee in FIG. 10).
The slope of the output-versus-current curve above threshold, expressed as photons out per electron in.
The ratio of a resonator's free spectral range to its linewidth. For small loss S per pass it is about pi/S.
A wafer whose surface is a (100) crystal plane, the standard orientation for GaAs epitaxy.
A surface treatment, here with sulfur or selenium, that removes surface states. On etched sidewalls these states would otherwise cause non-radiative recombination and leakage current.
